title: Ephemeral Ark Proxy: threadsafe degradation adapter for downstream resilience
creator: Marisol Vega
description:
Problem: During 3 recent incidents we saw cascading latency and retries originating from stateful downstreams (Redis and our Kafka write path). Connection pools were saturating under regional warm-up, causing long tails and client-side retries. Existing circuit/fallback behavior is coarse-grained and hard to enable for short-lived bursts. We need a lightweight, threadsafe, per-host ephemeral proxy layer ("Ark Proxy") that can quarantine misbehaving backends, return calibrated degraded responses or lightweight stubs, and gracefully reopen once health metrics recover.

This ticket captures the design and implementation plan for a threadsafe degradation adapter that sits between the runtime worker and downstream client(s). It focuses on: adaptive connection admission, per-host quarantine with staged stubs, coordinated multi-region failover soft-handoffs, and SLO-aware load-shedding policies.
proposal: Build an Ephemeral Ark Proxy library component embedded in the serving worker process. Responsibilities: (1) maintain a thin connection pool façade per downstream host with admission control, (2) track short-term health signals (p50/p95/p99 latencies, error rates, connection failures), (3) apply graduated quarantine states: OK -> Warning (shed noncritical reads/writes) -> Isolate (return stub/degraded response) -> Blackhole (reject), (4) provide hooks for multi-region failover orchestration (handoff token and preferred-region header), (5) expose telemetry for SLO evaluation and automated tuning. The library will be threadsafe and designed for minimal allocations in the hot path.
design_decisions: Connection façade per backend host instead of global pool: reduces blast radius and enables per-host quarantine
Short sliding window health metrics (30s) combined with exponential backoff for reopen attempts: balances sensitivity vs stability
Staged stubs: read-only endpoints return cached or synthetic responses; write paths return confirmation with async-enqueue where possible
Prefer conservative rejects for transactional DB writes; only permit degraded write stubbing behind explicit feature flag
Circuit state transitions are local but emit events to the control plane to allow cross-region coordination and visibility
tradeoffs: Per-host façades increase memory/descriptor usage compared to pooled global connectors, but reduce cross-tenant failure amplification
Returning stubs for reads improves client latency and SLOs but may decrease freshness/consistency — acceptable for some prompt caching but not for transactional operations
Adding an in-process proxy simplifies latency but duplicates some connection logic with existing clients — mitigated by small shared adapter layer and tests
Aggressive quarantine thresholds reduce tail-latency but may cause higher error rates at application layer if not tuned carefully
implementation_steps: 1) Define Ark Proxy API: admit(), call(), health_event(), metrics_export() — design doc link in attachments
2) Implement per-host façade with LRU of hosts to bound resource usage
3) Integrate latency/error rolling window (30s buckets) and state machine: OK/DEGRADED/ISOLATED/BLACKHOLE
4) Add per-request scoring: is_critical, can_stubbing_apply, tenant_priority for admission decisions
5) Implement staged stub strategies: cached read, synthetic placeholder, async-write-enqueue fallback
6) Add control-plane event emitter for cross-region coordination (emit via existing telemetry channel)
7) Add feature flags and runtime knobs (percentile thresholds, quarantine timers, max-stub-rate)
8) Unit + integration tests against fake Redis/Kafka/DB drivers; chaos tests for flapping backends
9) Canary rollout to low-traffic serving pool; monitor SLO and customer-facing errors
10) Iterate thresholds based on telemetry and incident postmortems
testing_plan: Unit tests for state transitions and concurrency invariants (thread-safety under 5000 concurrent calls)
Integration tests with local redis-server and kafkacat to validate quarantine and stub behaviors
Synthetic latency injection tests (p95/p99 spikes) to assert Ark Proxy moves to DEGRADED/ISOLATED appropriately
Chaos tests in staging: flapping connections, partial packet loss, induced connection limits
End-to-end canary with shadow traffic for 48h measuring token cost, request latency, and correctness of degraded responses
Regression tests to ensure transactional DB writes are never silently acknowledged when feature flag is off
monitoring_and_alerting: Dashboards: ArkProxy per-region per-backend state counts, quarantined-hosts, stub-rate, admission-drop-rate
SLOs: track 95th and 99th token-latency for requests that hit degraded paths vs OK paths
Alerts: high quarantined-host count (>5% hosts) per region, sustained stub-rate (>2% of requests) for >10m, spike in rejected writes
Link the ArkProxy events to existing tracing (trace id propagation) to simplify root-cause analysis
Expose metrics as labelled Prometheus metrics: ark_quarantine_state{region,backend_host,state}
rollout_plan: Phase 1: Library build + unit/integration tests (branch) — internal review and security check
Phase 2: Canary deploy to a single non-critical region with 1/10th traffic, enable read stubbing only
Phase 3: Gradually expand to additional regions and add DEGRADED write-yielding paths behind opt-in flags
Phase 4: Full rollout with automatic tuning and telemetry-driven threshold recommendations
Rollback criteria: more than 0.5% increase in customer-facing 5xx for 30m or inability to recover quarantined hosts after 30m
acceptance_criteria: Library implements API and passes unit + integration tests
Canary demonstrates reduced p99 tail latency by >=20% during induced backend latency events
No silent acknowledgment of transactional writes when feature flag is disabled
Telemetry surfaces ArkProxy state and matches postmortem expectations for at least 2 synthetic incidents
Documentation and runbook added to Confluence and on-call triage updated
notes: This approach complements higher-level regional failover orchestration (see ENG-31248) but focuses on localized containment
Expect an initial increase in descriptor usage; ops will monitor node fd counts and may adjust host LRU sizes
We should coordinate with platform security for any behavior that returns synthetic responses to ensure compliance
Plan to upstream the library as a small open-source shim after internal stabilization
